lessons.title: An extra early-diastolic sound
lessons.notice: Locate S1 and S2 first, then listen for a third sound early in diastole. S3 can be physiologic in some younger people; age and presentation matter.
lessons.difference: An added sound after S2.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left lower sternal border. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A low-pitched extra sound occurs just after S2. Which timing best describes this finding?
options: Early ventricular filling
Atrial contraction before S1
Ventricular ejection between S1 and S2
Inspiratory separation of the components of S2
questions.rationale: S3 follows S2 during early filling. S4 precedes S1; an ejection sound occurs during systole. A split S2 consists of two valve-closure components rather than a separate filling sound.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old has a newly detected S3, increasing orthopnea and a 2-kg weight gain in three days. Which interpretation best connects these findings?
options: Isolated age-related reduced ventricular compliance
Possible intravascular depletion after diuresis
Physiologic increased filling associated with exercise training
Possible worsening congestion requiring prompt assessment
questions.rationale: The symptom and weight trend make congestion the leading concern. Reduced compliance is more associated with S4. Depletion does not fit the weight gain and orthopnea; a physiologic S3 is more plausible in a healthy younger person.

questions.stem: Which assessment most directly helps evaluate whether a newly detected S3 is associated with pulmonary congestion?
options: Orthostatic blood pressure and positional dizziness
Peripheral pulse symmetry and capillary refill
Respiratory effort, oxygen saturation and dependent lung sounds
Apical-radial pulse comparison and rhythm regularity
questions.rationale: Breathing effort, oxygenation and basal crackles directly address pulmonary involvement. The other assessments assess rhythm, orthostasis or peripheral perfusion and remain useful, but answer different questions.

lessons.title: An extra late-diastolic sound
lessons.notice: Compare the interval before S1. The dataset labels this simulated extra sound S4; interpretation requires context.
lessons.difference: An added sound before S1.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at right costal margin. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: An extra low-pitched sound is heard immediately before S1. Which mechanism best fits its timing?
options: Rapid passive filling immediately after S2
Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve
Turbulent flow during ventricular ejection
Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
questions.rationale: S4 occurs with atrial contraction late in diastole. Rapid filling explains S3; delayed pulmonic closure affects S2 splitting, and ventricular ejection is systolic.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing hypertension has an S4 but no new dyspnea. Which additional finding would best support the proposed mechanism?
options: A respiratory variation in S2 splitting
An isolated increase in resting sinus rate
Left ventricular hypertrophy on a prior echocardiogram
A recent decrease in hemoglobin
questions.rationale: Hypertrophy can reduce ventricular compliance, supporting an S4 mechanism. Anemia or tachycardia may change flow sounds but do not specifically establish stiffness; respiratory S2 splitting concerns valve-closure timing.

questions.stem: A previously documented S4 is no longer heard after the patient develops atrial fibrillation. What best explains this change?
options: Earlier pulmonic valve closure
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction
Improved ventricular compliance
Reduced turbulence through the aortic valve
questions.rationale: An S4 requires coordinated atrial contraction, which is lost in atrial fibrillation. Its disappearance in this setting does not demonstrate improved ventricular compliance or a change in valve disease.

lessons.title: Early systolic murmur
lessons.notice: Use S1 and S2 as timing landmarks. Learn the timing pattern before trying to assign an underlying cause.
lessons.difference: Additional sound in early systole.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at right upper sternal border. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A murmur begins with S1 and ends well before S2. Which description fits?
options: Late systolic
Early diastolic
Early systolic
Holosystolic
questions.rationale: The beginning and end locate the murmur in early systole. Holosystolic spans S1 to S2; late systolic begins later, while early diastolic follows S2.

questions.stem: Two nurses disagree whether a short murmur occurs before or after S2. Which bedside approach most directly resolves the timing?
options: Compare the sound during inspiration and expiration
Identify S1 and S2 while correlating with a gently palpated single carotid pulse
Compare the sound over the apex and axilla for radiation
Grade the loudness with the patient supine
questions.rationale: The carotid upstroke occurs during systole and helps anchor timing. Radiation, intensity and respiratory variation characterize a murmur but do not directly resolve the systolic-versus-diastolic question.

questions.stem: A patient develops a new systolic murmur with chest pain, cool skin and falling blood pressure. Which response takes priority?
options: Activate urgent clinical evaluation while assessing circulation and breathing
Obtain a 12-lead ECG to characterize possible ischemia
Establish IV access for anticipated treatment
Prepare the patient for bedside echocardiography
questions.rationale: Chest pain with falling pressure and cool skin indicates instability. Escalation and immediate circulation/breathing assessment lead the response; ECG, IV access and echocardiography are important concurrent or subsequent steps, not prerequisites for calling for help.

lessons.title: Mid systolic murmur
lessons.notice: Listen for a sustained sound between the primary heart sounds. Loudness alone does not establish severity.
lessons.difference: Additional sound during the middle of systole.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at apex. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A murmur starts after S1, rises and falls in intensity, and ends before S2. Which pattern does this describe?
options: Late diastolic rumble
Midsystolic ejection murmur
Holosystolic regurgitant murmur
Early diastolic decrescendo murmur
questions.rationale: An ejection murmur occupies the middle of systole with a crescendo-decrescendo contour. Holosystolic sound spans systole; the other patterns occur after S2 and before the next S1.

questions.stem: A patient has an ejection-type murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border. Which additional finding most supports an aortic stenosis pattern?
options: Radiation toward the carotid arteries
Radiation from the apex toward the left axilla
Increasing intensity with inspiration at the lower sternal border
A low-pitched rumble at the apex in diastole
questions.rationale: Carotid radiation supports an aortic outflow pattern. Apical-to-axillary radiation suggests mitral regurgitation; inspiratory augmentation suggests a right-sided origin; a diastolic apical rumble is a different pattern. Echocardiography establishes the lesion.

questions.stem: Which history makes an ejection-type murmur more urgent to report for clinical evaluation?
options: Long-standing brief palpitations after caffeine
Stable ankle swelling after prolonged standing
Intermittent chest tenderness reproduced by palpation
Recent exertional syncope with chest pressure
questions.rationale: Exertional syncope and chest pressure raise concern for a hemodynamically significant outflow problem. The other histories merit assessment but are less specifically concerning for symptomatic outflow obstruction.

lessons.title: Late systolic murmur
lessons.notice: Compare when the additional sound appears within the cardiac cycle. Do not equate this sample with a specific valve diagnosis.
lessons.difference: Additional sound later in systole.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left upper sternal border. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A click is followed by a murmur during the final part of the S1-to-S2 interval. How should its timing be documented?
options: Late systolic
Early systolic
Early diastolic
Presystolic diastolic
questions.rationale: The sound remains before S2, so it is systolic, despite occurring late in the interval. Presystolic means late diastole before the next S1.

questions.stem: A stable patient has an apical midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur. Which condition is most consistent with that pattern?
options: Aortic valve stenosis
Mitral valve stenosis
Aortic valve regurgitation
Mitral valve prolapse
questions.rationale: A midsystolic click with a late systolic apical murmur supports mitral valve prolapse. Aortic stenosis generally produces an ejection pattern; mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation produce characteristic diastolic murmurs.

questions.stem: A click midway between S1 and S2 is followed by a murmur that continues to S2 in an asymptomatic patient. Which handoff most accurately describes it?
options: Low-pitched apical sound after S2 during early filling; no new symptoms
Brief apical sound just before S1 with no sustained murmur; no new symptoms
Apical click followed by a murmur ending at S2; no new dyspnea or chest pain
Apical murmur beginning at S1 and continuing uniformly to S2; no new symptoms
questions.rationale: The click followed by a murmur ending at S2 describes the late systolic pattern. The alternatives describe a holosystolic murmur, S3-like timing or S4-like timing. Timing must match what was actually heard.

lessons.title: Late diastolic murmur
lessons.notice: Compare the interval approaching the next S1. A new murmur warrants clinical assessment rather than diagnosis from audio alone.
lessons.difference: Additional sound late in diastole.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left costal margin. They are amplified teaching examples, not a recording of the learner’s patient.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms, vital signs and perfusion; document the sound and location and communicate new or concerning findings through the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A low-pitched rumble occurs near the end of the S2-to-next-S1 interval. Which phase is involved?
options: Early ventricular ejection
Late ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric contraction after S1
Late ventricular filling
questions.rationale: The interval after S2 and before the next S1 is diastole. A rumble near its end is late diastolic, while the other choices describe systolic events.

questions.stem: A stable patient has an apical low-pitched diastolic rumble. Which technique best helps assess it?
options: Diaphragm at the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward
Bell at the left upper sternal border during inspiration
Bell lightly applied with the patient in the left lateral position
Diaphragm firmly applied at the right upper sternal border
questions.rationale: Light bell pressure at the apex in the left lateral position favors low-pitched mitral-area sounds. The other positions are useful for different valve areas or higher-pitched sounds.

questions.stem: Which accompanying finding most supports a mitral stenosis pattern rather than an aortic regurgitation pattern?
options: Early diastolic sound best heard while leaning forward
Opening snap followed by an apical diastolic rumble
High-pitched decrescendo sound along the left sternal border
Bounding peripheral pulses with a widened pulse pressure
questions.rationale: An opening snap and apical rumble support mitral stenosis. The other findings fit an aortic regurgitation pattern. These findings guide evaluation; echocardiography is needed to characterize valve disease.

lessons.title: Wheeze
lessons.notice: Listen across a full breathing cycle. Wheeze is a sound description and does not by itself establish asthma.
lessons.difference: A continuous musical added sound.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left upper anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A continuous musical sound is louder during expiration. Which description best fits?
options: Pleural friction rub
Coarse crackles
Wheeze
Fine crackles
questions.rationale: A wheeze is a sustained musical sound associated with narrowed airways. Crackles are interrupted pops; a rub is a localized grating sound linked to pleural movement.

questions.stem: After an inhaled bronchodilator, which combination best supports improvement in a patient with wheezing?
options: Fewer audible sounds with a rising respiratory rate
Less work of breathing, better air entry and easier speech
Quieter wheezing with weaker air entry and increasing fatigue
Higher oxygen saturation with increasing somnolence
questions.rationale: Improvement requires evidence of better ventilation and reduced effort. Reduced wheezing alone can reflect less airflow; worsening fatigue, somnolence or tachypnea argues against recovery.

questions.stem: A patient with an asthma exacerbation has very little air movement, fading wheezes and increasing exhaustion. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Urgent escalation for possible respiratory failure
Repeat the prescribed rescue treatment and reassess its effect
Measure peak expiratory flow to quantify obstruction
Obtain an arterial blood gas to quantify carbon dioxide retention
questions.rationale: Poor air movement with exhaustion suggests threatened respiratory failure. Activate urgent help and support breathing; treatment and diagnostic measurements may occur in parallel but should not delay escalation.

lessons.title: Fine crackles
lessons.notice: Compare the discrete interruptions with the smooth reference recording. Disease attribution requires the full assessment.
lessons.difference: Brief discontinuous added sounds.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left upper anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Short, high-pitched popping sounds occur near the end of inspiration and persist after coughing. Which finding best fits?
options: Pleural friction rub
Fine crackles
Rhonchi
Expiratory wheeze
questions.rationale: Fine crackles are brief, discontinuous inspiratory sounds. Rhonchi are lower and more continuous; wheezes are musical, and a rub has a grating quality.

questions.stem: An older patient has new bilateral basal fine crackles, orthopnea and rapid weight gain. Which explanation best integrates these findings?
options: Pulmonary congestion associated with fluid accumulation
Upper-airway narrowing associated with laryngeal edema
Large-airway secretions associated with ineffective coughing
Unilateral pleural air associated with a collapsed lung
questions.rationale: The distribution and fluid-related symptoms support pulmonary congestion. Upper-airway narrowing, secretions and unilateral pleural air have different assessment patterns.

questions.stem: Fine crackles are newly detected at both bases. Which reassessment best determines whether the patient is deteriorating now?
options: Compare morning and evening ankle circumference
Review the sodium content of the previous meals
Review prior pulmonary-function test results
Compare respiratory effort, saturation and oxygen requirement with baseline
questions.rationale: Current breathing and oxygen-support trends show immediate respiratory impact. Edema, diet and historical testing provide context but are less direct measures of acute deterioration.

lessons.title: Coarse crackles
lessons.notice: The curated dataset labels this example coarse crackles. Sound terminology and perceived quality need independent review.
lessons.difference: Coarser discontinuous added sounds.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left lower anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Low-pitched bubbling, interrupted sounds are heard during inspiration. Which description best fits?
options: Coarse crackles
Fine crackles
Rhonchi
Wheeze
questions.rationale: Coarse crackles are discontinuous and relatively low-pitched. Rhonchi can also be low-pitched but are more continuous and snoring; fine crackles are shorter and higher-pitched.

questions.stem: A stable patient has coarse crackles and a productive cough. What reassessment most directly tests whether mobilized secretions contribute to the sounds?
options: Compare percussion over the apices and bases
Repeat auscultation while the patient briefly holds their breath
Compare apical and radial pulse rates
Re-auscultate the same sites after an effective cough
questions.rationale: A change after coughing supports a secretion contribution. Percussion assesses underlying density; a breath hold removes airflow, and pulse comparison does not evaluate secretion clearance.

questions.stem: Coarse crackles persist in a patient with a weak cough and increasing oxygen needs. Which concern should guide the next nursing assessment?
options: Whether the sound is louder with the stethoscope bell
Whether the patient has chronic exercise intolerance
Ability to clear secretions and maintain ventilation
Presence of a pleural rub with breath holding
questions.rationale: Weak cough and increasing support needs raise concern about airway clearance and ventilation. Refining sound technique or chronic history should not displace assessment of the current respiratory problem.

lessons.title: Rhonchi
lessons.notice: Describe the sound, site and phase. Reassessment after coughing may provide information but is not a diagnosis.
lessons.difference: A lower-pitched continuous added sound.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at left upper anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A low-pitched snoring sound continues through much of expiration and changes after coughing. Which finding best fits?
options: Fine crackles
Pleural friction rub
Stridor
Rhonchi
questions.rationale: Rhonchi are relatively continuous low-pitched sounds often associated with larger-airway secretions. Fine crackles are interrupted, a rub is grating, and stridor is usually prominent over the neck.

questions.stem: A patient with rhonchi coughs up sputum. Which reassessment most directly evaluates the immediate effect?
options: Temperature trend and white blood cell count
Fluid intake and the previous day’s weight
Air entry, work of breathing and sounds at the same lung sites
Sputum color and the previous antibiotic schedule
questions.rationale: Repeat examination of breathing and the same sites evaluates clearance. Sputum, infection markers and fluid balance are useful context but do not directly show the immediate respiratory response.

questions.stem: Which finding would most strongly shift concern from lower-airway secretions to an upper-airway problem?
options: Brief end-inspiratory pops at both posterior bases
Harsh inspiratory sound loudest over the neck with voice change
Low-pitched chest sounds that decrease after coughing
Bilateral musical expiratory sounds across several lung fields
questions.rationale: Neck-predominant inspiratory noise with voice change suggests upper-airway narrowing. The alternatives describe rhonchi, wheezing or crackles and warrant different focused assessments.

lessons.title: Pleural friction rub
lessons.notice: Listen for the coarse rubbing quality alongside the breath cycle. Similar-sounding artifacts must be considered.
lessons.difference: A grating added sound.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at right mid anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A localized grating sound occurs during inspiration and expiration and does not clear with coughing. Which finding best fits?
options: Fine crackles
Expiratory wheeze
Pleural friction rub
Rhonchi
questions.rationale: A pleural rub is a localized rough sound caused by pleural surfaces moving. Rhonchi may change after coughing; crackles are brief pops and wheezes are musical.

questions.stem: A stable patient has a scratchy sound near the left lower chest. What observation helps distinguish a pleural rub from a pericardial rub?
options: Whether the sound is audible only with the bell
Whether the sound stops during a brief breath hold
Whether the sound increases after drinking water
Whether the sound is louder over clothing
questions.rationale: A pleural rub depends on respiration and stops when breathing stops; a pericardial rub can persist with cardiac motion. The other comparisons do not reliably distinguish these sources.

questions.stem: A patient with pleuritic pain and a suspected rub develops sudden dyspnea, tachycardia and falling saturation. What takes priority?
options: Urgent assessment and escalation of the acute respiratory change
Obtain a 12-lead ECG to evaluate another source of chest pain
Prepare for the requested chest radiograph
Give prescribed analgesia to reduce painful splinting
questions.rationale: New hypoxemia and respiratory distress need immediate assessment and escalation. ECG, imaging and pain control can all be appropriate, but none should delay the response to deterioration.

lessons.title: Wheeze at a lower anterior site
lessons.notice: Practice recognizing the finding in another recording and location; this is another example of wheeze, not a new disease.
lessons.difference: A wheeze in a second auscultation location.
lessons.context: Matched manikin recordings at right lower anterior. A normal comparator does not rule out respiratory illness.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess respiratory effort, rate, symptoms and oxygenation; compare sites and escalate respiratory distress according to the local pathway.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A wheeze is heard at the right lower anterior chest. Which next comparison best determines its distribution?
options: Measure chest circumference at full inspiration
Listen at matching left-sided and additional posterior sites
Listen repeatedly at the same site using greater pressure
Compare the apical pulse with the radial pulse
questions.rationale: Comparing symmetric and additional sites establishes focal versus diffuse distribution. Repeating one site or measuring pulses or circumference does not map the sound.

questions.stem: A persistent focal wheeze is heard in the same location after coughing, while other fields are clear. Which possibility deserves particular consideration?
options: Localized airway obstruction
Diffuse small-airway narrowing
Bilateral interstitial fluid accumulation
Diffuse pleural inflammation
questions.rationale: Persistent focal findings warrant evaluation for a local airway process. Diffuse airway or interstitial processes more often produce broader distributions, although the sound alone cannot establish the cause.

questions.stem: A child suddenly coughs while eating, then has a new unilateral wheeze. Which history detail is most important to communicate promptly?
options: A family history of seasonal allergies
An earlier episode of exercise-related coughing
A mild cold that resolved the previous week
Abrupt onset during eating with possible aspiration
questions.rationale: The abrupt event during eating raises concern for an inhaled foreign body and needs prompt airway assessment. Allergic and viral histories are relevant but less specific to this sudden focal change.

lessons.title: Stage 1 pressure injury
lessons.notice: Evaluate color change relative to baseline and nearby skin, plus temperature, firmness and sensation. Redness can be less visible in darker skin.
lessons.difference: Intact skin with persistent nonblanchable change.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: After pressure over the sacrum, skin remains intact with a localized nonblanchable area. There is no purple or maroon discoloration. Which classification best fits?
options: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Deep tissue pressure injury
Moisture-associated skin damage
questions.rationale: Intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema supports stage 1. Stage 2 requires partial-thickness loss; deep red, maroon or purple changes suggest deep tissue injury. Moisture damage requires a different causal assessment.

questions.stem: On deeply pigmented skin, redness over a pressure point is difficult to see. Which additional assessment is most useful?
options: Use the absence of visible redness to lower the pressure-risk score
Estimate wound depth from the degree of color contrast
Classify the site using a photograph taken with flash
Compare local warmth, firmness and tenderness with adjacent tissue
questions.rationale: Temperature, consistency and sensation changes can supplement visual assessment across skin tones. Color alone and flash photographs cannot establish depth or exclude pressure-related injury.

questions.stem: A bedbound patient has a new nonblanchable area over the heel. Which intervention most directly addresses the cause?
options: Request a nutrition assessment for healing support
Increase the frequency of documented skin inspection
Offload the heel and reassess the affected tissue
Apply a prophylactic foam dressing over the heel
questions.rationale: Offloading directly reduces the pressure causing injury. A protective dressing, nutrition assessment and closer surveillance can complement care but do not replace pressure relief.

lessons.title: Stage 2 pressure injury
lessons.notice: Do not use this stage for moisture damage, adhesive injury, burns or skin tears. Confirm pressure/shear context.
lessons.difference: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A sacral pressure injury has partial-thickness skin loss with exposed moist pink dermis. No adipose, slough or deeper tissue is visible. Which classification fits?
options: Stage 3
Unstageable
Deep tissue pressure injury
Stage 2
questions.rationale: Exposed dermis without deeper tissue or obscuring material supports stage 2. Visible adipose indicates deeper loss; obscured full-thickness injury is unstageable, and persistent deep discoloration suggests deep tissue injury.

questions.stem: A patient with frequent liquid stools has diffuse superficial perineal erosion with irregular edges, extending beyond pressure points. Which finding most supports moisture-associated damage rather than a stage 2 pressure injury?
options: Pain reported during cleansing
Superficial loss of the epidermis
Distribution corresponding to repeated stool exposure
A moist pink surface in the affected area
questions.rationale: Exposure history and distribution help distinguish moisture injury. A pink surface, pain and superficial skin loss can occur in both and cannot independently establish pressure as the cause.

questions.stem: An injury was recorded as stage 2. During cleansing, the nurse identifies yellow adipose tissue in the wound bed. What is the best interpretation?
options: The wound is deep tissue injury because fat is now visible
The wound extends beyond the depth allowed for stage 2
The wound remains stage 2 because no bone is exposed
The wound is unstageable because any yellow tissue obscures depth
questions.rationale: Visible adipose indicates full-thickness loss and is incompatible with stage 2. Fat is different from slough; stage 4 requires deeper exposed or palpable structures. Reassessment should establish the deepest involved tissue.

lessons.title: Stage 3 pressure injury
lessons.notice: Visible depth varies by anatomical site. Exposed fascia, muscle, tendon or bone would not fit stage 3.
lessons.difference: Full-thickness skin loss extending into fat.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A pressure injury has visible adipose and granulation tissue. Its full depth is visible, with no exposed or directly palpable fascia, muscle, tendon or bone. Which stage fits?
options: Stage 4
Unstageable
Stage 3
Stage 2
questions.rationale: Full-thickness loss with adipose but without exposed or directly palpable deeper structures fits stage 3. Stage 2 is shallower; stage 4 involves deeper structures, and unstageable means the extent is obscured.

questions.stem: A stage 3 injury has undermining at one edge. Which documentation best supports repeat assessment?
options: Drainage color without the tissue-depth findings
Clock-face location and measured extent of the undermining
Surface length and width without the undermining extent
A photograph without a scale or orientation
questions.rationale: Undermining can extend beyond the surface opening. Recording its location and extent complements surface dimensions and permits meaningful comparison; photographs or drainage descriptions alone miss that geometry.

questions.stem: Two stage 3 injuries have different measured depths, one over an area with little fat and one over an adipose-rich area. Why can both have the same stage?
options: Stage reflects involved tissue layers, while anatomical depth varies by site
Stage depends primarily on surface area rather than involved tissue
Stage depends primarily on how long the injury has been present
Stage reflects drainage volume rather than anatomical depth
questions.rationale: Staging describes tissue involvement rather than a universal depth in centimeters. Body site and adipose thickness change measured depth; size, duration and drainage are separately documented characteristics.

lessons.title: Stage 4 pressure injury
lessons.notice: A diagram cannot establish the deepest tissue involved. Assessment and wound-care review are required.
lessons.difference: Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed or palpable deeper structures.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A pressure injury contains directly palpable tendon at its base. Which classification best fits?
options: Deep tissue pressure injury
Stage 4
Stage 3
Unstageable
questions.rationale: Exposed or directly palpable tendon is a stage 4 feature. Stage 3 lacks exposed deeper structures; an obscured base without known extent is unstageable. Deep tissue injury describes a different presentation.

questions.stem: A previously documented stage 4 injury is filling with granulation tissue and now appears shallow. How should it be described?
options: Healing stage 4 pressure injury with current dimensions
Stage 3 pressure injury because the deep structures are covered
Stage 2 pressure injury because the surface is now shallow
Unstageable pressure injury because granulation covers the base
questions.rationale: Pressure injuries are not reverse-staged during healing. Preserve the known deepest stage and document current tissue and dimensions; healthy granulation is not obscuring slough or eschar.

questions.stem: A patient with a stage 4 injury develops new confusion, fever and hypotension. Which response has priority?
options: Obtain ordered blood cultures for suspected infection
Establish IV access for anticipated fluids and medication
Measure wound dimensions and inspect for local spread
Urgent escalation for possible systemic infection and instability
questions.rationale: Confusion, fever and hypotension require urgent escalation and assessment of instability. Cultures, IV access and focused wound assessment may be needed promptly, but are parts of the response rather than reasons to delay calling for help.

lessons.title: Unstageable pressure injury
lessons.notice: Do not guess stage 3 or 4 through obscuring slough or eschar. Follow local wound assessment and escalation guidance.
lessons.difference: Obscured full-thickness injury whose depth cannot be determined.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A pressure injury has full-thickness tissue loss, but adherent slough covers the base and prevents assessment of its extent. Which classification is appropriate?
options: Unstageable pressure injury
Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 4 pressure injury
Deep tissue pressure injury
questions.rationale: When slough or eschar prevents determining full depth, the injury is unstageable. Stage 3 or 4 cannot be assigned from an obscured base without sufficient evidence of the involved structures.

questions.stem: A heel has dry, adherent, intact eschar without erythema or fluctuance. Which plan best fits this finding?
options: Moisten the eschar to accelerate softening at the bedside
Remove the edge during routine cleansing to identify the stage
Cover with a moisture-retentive product specifically to promote removal
Offload and monitor; seek wound and perfusion guidance before removal
questions.rationale: Stable heel eschar should not be softened or removed simply to expose the base. Offloading, monitoring and assessment of perfusion and wound needs guide management; instability or infection signs change the evaluation.

questions.stem: After clinically indicated debridement, an unstageable pressure injury has visible adipose but no exposed or palpable deeper structures, and its full extent is visible. How should it now be classified?
options: Stage 4
Deep tissue pressure injury
Stage 3
Stage 2
questions.rationale: Once the extent can be assessed, visible adipose without deeper exposed or palpable structures supports stage 3. Debridement reveals depth; it does not make the original full-thickness injury a stage 2 wound.

lessons.title: Deep tissue pressure injury
lessons.notice: Intact or nonintact skin may be present. Temperature or sensation changes can precede a visible color change; appearance varies with skin tone.
lessons.difference: Persistent deep red, maroon or purple discoloration with underlying tissue concern.
lessons.context: Original schematic, not a patient photograph. Staging requires history, examination and assessment of the tissue involved.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess skin and pressure/shear exposure, document findings and seek qualified wound assessment; follow the individualized pressure-relief plan.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: After prolonged pressure, a heel has persistent nonblanchable maroon discoloration under intact skin. Which classification best fits?
options: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
Deep tissue pressure injury
questions.rationale: Persistent maroon or purple discoloration after pressure suggests deep tissue injury. Stage 1 lacks these deep discoloration features, stage 2 exposes dermis, and unstageable injury has obscuring slough or eschar.

questions.stem: A patient has a purple area after striking their shin against a chair. Which assessment is most important before labeling it deep tissue pressure injury?
options: Use the intensity of the purple color to infer wound depth
Classify it according to whether the skin surface is intact
Determine whether pressure or shear, rather than trauma, explains the injury
Measure the purple area and stage it according to its diameter
questions.rationale: Pressure-injury classification requires an appropriate mechanism. Bruising from trauma can resemble deep discoloration; color, size and intact skin alone do not establish a pressure injury.

questions.stem: A suspected deep tissue pressure injury remains intact but becomes more painful and boggy. What is the best nursing response?
options: Wait for the surface to open before updating the care plan
Maintain offloading, document changes and request prompt wound reassessment
Reclassify as stage 1 because the surface remains intact
Reclassify as stage 2 because pain has increased
questions.rationale: Deep damage can evolve beneath an intact surface. Increasing pain and consistency changes require reassessment and pressure relief; neither pain nor intact skin alone determines a new stage.

lessons.title: Chest X-ray: pneumothorax
lessons.notice: The source image includes an arrow indicating the edge of the collapsed lung.
lessons.difference: A pleural line with reduced peripheral lung markings.
lessons.context: Different patients and acquisition conditions; the abnormal source is an expiratory film. Projection and inspiration affect appearance.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: On an upright chest radiograph, a thin pleural line is visible with no lung markings peripheral to it. Which finding best fits?
options: Lobar consolidation
Pulmonary edema
Pneumothorax
Pleural effusion
questions.rationale: A pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings suggests air in the pleural space. Effusion causes fluid opacity; consolidation and edema increase pulmonary opacity rather than create a peripheral air space.

questions.stem: After a central-line procedure, a patient develops sudden dyspnea and markedly reduced breath sounds on one side. Which associated finding makes escalation especially urgent?
options: A small area of bruising around the dressing
Falling blood pressure with worsening respiratory distress
Mild discomfort limited to the insertion site
A stable oxygen requirement with unchanged respiratory effort
questions.rationale: Respiratory deterioration with hypotension raises concern for a life-threatening complication, including tension physiology. Urgent escalation must not wait for confirmatory imaging; local discomfort or bruising has a different risk pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with a known small pneumothorax is being observed. Which trend is most important to report promptly?
options: Increasing oxygen requirement with new tachypnea
Unchanged discomfort on deep inspiration
Stable heart rate during quiet rest
No change in the insertion-site dressing
questions.rationale: Increasing respiratory support and tachypnea suggest worsening physiological impact. Stable pain, pulse or dressing findings do not offset respiratory deterioration.

lessons.title: Chest X-ray: pleural effusion
lessons.notice: Use the source annotations to locate the effusion; correlate with the radiology report.
lessons.difference: Fluid-related opacity and change in the costophrenic region.
lessons.context: These are different patients and are not a before-and-after pair. A single image is not a full examination.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: An upright chest radiograph shows blunting of a costophrenic angle and a curved upper fluid margin. Which finding best fits?
options: Focal upper-lobe cavitation
Pleural effusion
Pneumothorax
Hyperinflation
questions.rationale: Dependent fluid may blunt the costophrenic angle and form a meniscus. Pneumothorax produces a pleural air pattern; hyperinflation and cavitation have different radiographic appearances.

questions.stem: Which bedside finding is most consistent with a moderate pleural effusion at the affected base?
options: Dull percussion with diminished breath sounds
Hyperresonance with diminished breath sounds
Diffuse expiratory wheezing with prolonged expiration
Loud bronchial breathing over a focal air-space opacity
questions.rationale: Pleural fluid dampens breath sounds and produces dullness. Hyperresonance suggests excess air; diffuse wheeze suggests airway narrowing, and bronchial breathing may occur over consolidation.

questions.stem: A patient becomes acutely dyspneic with new unilateral reduction in breath sounds after thoracentesis. What is the priority?
options: Prepare the patient for an urgent chest radiograph
Check the drainage record and procedure documentation
Assess the puncture site for bleeding or fluid leakage
Prompt respiratory assessment and escalation for a possible complication
questions.rationale: Acute dyspnea and unilateral reduction in breath sounds require immediate respiratory assessment and escalation. Imaging, procedure review and site inspection can help identify the complication, but should not delay stabilizing assessment.

lessons.title: Head CT: subdural collection
lessons.notice: Identify the modality and orientation before examining the area of concern.
lessons.difference: An extra-axial collection in the source-labeled subdural example.
lessons.context: Different individuals and slice levels. The reference is a noncontrast axial head CT; scan settings and displayed windowing can differ. A single slice cannot exclude injury or establish a diagnosis.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: An acute head CT shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense extra-axial collection along the cerebral convexity. Which collection best fits this description?
options: Subdural hematoma
Epidural hematoma
Intraparenchymal hematoma
Intraventricular hemorrhage
questions.rationale: A crescentic collection along the convexity supports subdural blood. Epidural blood is typically lentiform; intraparenchymal and intraventricular blood occupy different anatomical compartments.

questions.stem: A patient under observation after a head injury becomes harder to awaken and develops unequal pupils. Which action takes priority?
options: Measure bedside glucose to assess a reversible cause of reduced alertness
Prepare transport for repeat head CT
Review recent sedatives and analgesics for medication effects
Urgent escalation with repeat neurological and airway assessment
questions.rationale: Declining consciousness with new pupil asymmetry needs urgent neurological and airway assessment and escalation. Glucose, medication review and repeat imaging are useful parts of the evaluation, but must not delay help for the neurological change.

questions.stem: An older adult with a recent minor head injury reports a worsening headache. Which medication history most directly increases concern for intracranial bleeding?
options: Use of a proton-pump inhibitor
Use of a topical corticosteroid
Use of an oral anticoagulant
Use of an inhaled bronchodilator
questions.rationale: Anticoagulant use increases bleeding concern and is essential to communicate. The other medication classes do not carry the same direct implication for intracranial hemorrhage risk in this scenario.

lessons.title: Brain MRI: T2 abnormal signal
lessons.notice: Both examples are axial T2-weighted images. Compare symmetry, tissue signal and the ventricular region, then read the formal report. This image alone cannot determine the tumor type.
lessons.difference: Abnormal T2 signal and tissue distortion in a source-labeled brain-tumor example.
lessons.context: Different patients and slice levels. Both are T2-weighted, but acquisition settings and image resolution differ. An isolated slice cannot establish or exclude a diagnosis.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A T2 brain MRI has a region of increased signal with surrounding mass effect. What does mass effect describe?
options: The brightness of cerebrospinal fluid on T2 imaging
The concentration of contrast material in a vessel
The rate at which the scanner acquired the sequence
Displacement or compression of adjacent structures
questions.rationale: Mass effect refers to pressure-related displacement or compression. Signal brightness and acquisition parameters are different imaging properties; brightness alone is not mass effect.

questions.stem: A patient awaiting brain MRI has an implanted cardiac device but no device identification information available. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Use a lower-strength scanner without confirming device conditions
Substitute a noncontrast sequence to address the device concern
Verify the device and MRI conditions with the imaging team before entry
Remove external metal and proceed with the scheduled scan
questions.rationale: Implant identity and scanning conditions must be established by the MRI team. External metal removal, avoiding contrast or choosing a field strength does not independently establish implant safety.

questions.stem: A patient being evaluated for a brain lesion develops a new focal seizure and remains less responsive afterward. What is the immediate priority?
options: Record the duration and focal features of the seizure
Protect from injury, assess airway and breathing, and summon urgent help
Check bedside glucose for a reversible seizure trigger
Prepare the prescribed rescue medication for administration
questions.rationale: Immediate protection, airway/breathing assessment and urgent assistance lead the response. Glucose testing, prescribed rescue therapy and accurate observations are also important and can occur alongside that response.

lessons.title: Ultrasound: gallbladder findings
lessons.notice: The abnormal source describes an impacted stone and wall thickening. Review the report alongside the image.
lessons.difference: Echogenic material and posterior shadowing in a source-labeled stone example.
lessons.context: Different patients and scan planes. The reference shows a source-labeled normal gallbladder and common bile duct. A static image cannot replace a complete ultrasound examination.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A gallbladder ultrasound shows bright intraluminal foci that move with position and cast posterior acoustic shadows. Which finding best fits?
options: Simple fluid
Biliary sludge without stones
Gallstones
Gallbladder polyps
questions.rationale: Mobile echogenic foci with shadowing support stones. Polyps are attached to the wall; simple fluid is anechoic, and sludge generally layers without the classic stone shadow.

questions.stem: A patient has right upper-quadrant pain and gallstones on ultrasound. Which additional finding raises concern for acute inflammation rather than uncomplicated biliary colic?
options: An incidental stone in an asymptomatic patient
Persistent pain with fever and focal tenderness
Brief post-meal pain that has fully resolved
Intermittent discomfort without fever or tenderness
questions.rationale: Persistent symptoms with fever and focal tenderness increase concern for inflammatory disease and warrant prompt evaluation. Stones alone or brief resolved pain do not establish acute cholecystitis.

questions.stem: A patient with biliary pain develops fever, jaundice and hypotension. Which response is the priority?
options: Urgent escalation for possible infected biliary obstruction and instability
Obtain the ordered blood cultures and lactate
Establish IV access for anticipated therapy
Prepare for urgent biliary imaging
questions.rationale: Fever, jaundice and hypotension raise concern for an unstable biliary infection. Urgent escalation and assessment lead the response; cultures, IV access and imaging support it and should not become prerequisites for calling for help.

lessons.title: Ultrasound: collecting-system dilation
lessons.notice: Locate the renal outline and collecting system. Document report findings without inferring the cause from one image.
lessons.difference: Dilation of the collecting system in the abnormal example.
lessons.context: The abnormal source is pediatric; the normal reference age is not specified. These are anatomical comparisons, not matched demographic controls.
lessons.nursingAction: Review the formal report, assess symptoms and relevant observations, and communicate urgent findings through the local pathway. Do not clear a device or make a diagnosis from this lesson.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Renal ultrasound describes dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces. Which term matches the report?
options: Simple renal cyst
Hydronephrosis
Nephrolithiasis
Renal cortical thinning
questions.rationale: Hydronephrosis describes collecting-system dilation. A stone can cause it but is a separate finding; cortical thinning and a focal cyst describe different structures.

questions.stem: A patient with flank pain and collecting-system dilation develops fever, rigors and falling blood pressure. Which concern takes priority?
options: Possible infection with urinary obstruction
Uncomplicated renal colic without infection
Chronic dilation without current physiological impact
Isolated lower urinary symptoms without systemic illness
questions.rationale: Systemic infection signs with possible obstruction require urgent escalation. The new hypotension and rigors are incompatible with treating this as uncomplicated colic or an incidental chronic finding.

questions.stem: A patient has bilateral collecting-system dilation and reduced urine output. Which information most directly helps assess the effect on kidney function?
options: Urine color and odor at a single observation
A single blood pressure from the previous week
A history of occasional nocturia without recent change
Creatinine trend and measured urine output over time
questions.rationale: Serial creatinine and quantified urine output assess functional impact. Color, odor and older or nonspecific symptoms may add context but cannot establish current kidney function.

lessons.title: CBC: low hemoglobin
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: Hemoglobin below the displayed reference interval.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms and bleeding history, compare previous results, and communicate the change; do not infer the cause or a transfusion threshold from this number.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, below the report’s 12–16 g/dL interval. A patient reports fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Which interpretation best connects the result and symptoms?
options: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
Reduced platelet-mediated clot formation
Reduced neutrophil-mediated infection defense
Reduced renal clearance of metabolic waste
questions.rationale: Hemoglobin carries oxygen, so a low concentration can contribute to exertional symptoms. Platelets, neutrophils and renal filtration address different functions and require different measurements.

questions.stem: A patient has hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Why can anemia-related symptoms still occur?
options: Pulse oximetry directly measures oxygen dissolved in plasma rather than hemoglobin
Normal saturation indicates that tissue oxygen delivery is independent of hemoglobin
Anemia primarily impairs carbon dioxide removal rather than oxygen transport
Saturation measures the proportion of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, not its total amount
questions.rationale: A high percentage saturation can coexist with too little hemoglobin. Pulse oximetry does not measure total oxygen content or guarantee adequate tissue delivery.

questions.stem: Which assessment finding makes a newly low hemoglobin result most urgent to escalate?
options: Pallor without a change in vital signs
A history of low dietary iron intake
New chest pain with tachycardia and hypotension
Fatigue during activity that has been stable for months
questions.rationale: Chest pain and impaired perfusion indicate acute physiological compromise. Chronic fatigue, pallor and dietary history help investigate anemia but do not carry the same immediate urgency.

lessons.title: Potassium: elevated result
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: Potassium above the displayed reference interval.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Promptly assess the patient and follow the critical-result pathway. Check specimen quality and the reported result without dismissing it as artifact.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Potassium is 6.2 mmol/L in a nonhemolyzed sample, compared with 4.2 previously. Which assessment is most time-sensitive?
options: Daily weight and peripheral edema distribution
Dietary potassium intake during the preceding week
Bowel pattern and recent abdominal discomfort
Cardiac rhythm and current clinical stability
questions.rationale: Elevated potassium can cause dangerous conduction disturbances, making rhythm and stability assessment urgent. Fluid, diet and gastrointestinal history may help explain the result but do not assess its most immediate hazard.

questions.stem: A stable patient has an unexpectedly high potassium result flagged as hemolyzed. Which response best addresses the uncertainty?
options: Treat the result as artifact and wait for the next routine blood draw
Use the previous normal potassium as the current value
Assess the patient and arrange a prompt repeat sample while notifying the responsible clinician
Treat the result as confirmed and proceed without checking specimen quality
questions.rationale: Hemolysis can falsely elevate potassium, but true hyperkalemia may coexist. Clinical assessment, communication and prompt verification avoid both dismissing a dangerous value and treating an unverified artifact as certain.

questions.stem: A patient with elevated potassium has a normal initial ECG. Which interpretation is best?
options: The potassium can be rechecked at the next routine visit
A normal tracing does not remove the need for prompt potassium management
The potassium result is most likely due to specimen hemolysis
The risk is limited to skeletal muscle weakness until ECG changes occur
questions.rationale: ECG changes are not a sufficiently sensitive screen to exclude risk. A normal tracing does not prove artifact or justify delaying evaluation and management of a significant elevation.

lessons.title: CBC: low platelets
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: Platelets below the displayed reference interval.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess for bleeding and trends and communicate findings using the local pathway. A count alone does not identify the cause.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Platelets are 48 × 10⁹/L, with an illustrative interval of 150–400 × 10⁹/L. Which new symptom most directly fits impaired primary hemostasis?
options: Fever with purulent sputum
Polyuria with intense thirst
Petechiae with gingival bleeding
Exertional dyspnea with pallor
questions.rationale: Platelet deficiency commonly produces mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae and gum bleeding. The other patterns suggest anemia, infection or a metabolic problem rather than platelet function.

questions.stem: A patient with thrombocytopenia reports a sudden severe headache after a fall. Which response takes priority?
options: Request a repeat platelet count and compare with baseline
Urgent neurological assessment and escalation for possible bleeding
Apply fall precautions and assist the patient back to bed
Inspect for bruising and bleeding at other sites
questions.rationale: A sudden severe headache after a fall raises concern for intracranial bleeding. Neurological assessment and escalation take priority; fall precautions, other bleeding checks and repeat counts cannot exclude this complication.

questions.stem: Which planned activity most needs clarification for a patient with platelets of 48 × 10⁹/L?
options: A nonurgent intramuscular injection
A peripheral venipuncture with prolonged pressure afterward
A soft-toothbrush oral-care session
A supervised walk using the prescribed mobility aid
questions.rationale: A nonurgent intramuscular injection warrants clarification because it can cause a deep hematoma and alternatives may exist. Necessary venipuncture with pressure, gentle oral care and assisted mobility can be appropriate with individualized precautions.

lessons.title: Kidney report: rising creatinine
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: A rise from baseline in the stated time window.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Compare the 48-hour trend, urine output and clinical context, and communicate the change for assessment.

sources.title: AAFP · Acute kidney injury diagnosis and management

objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: Creatinine rises from 0.9 to 1.8 mg/dL over 48 hours. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: A change that can be interpreted only after symptoms develop
An acute change requiring evaluation for kidney injury
A stable result because 1.8 is less than twice the upper reference limit
Evidence of chronic kidney disease based on duration alone
questions.rationale: The rapid doubling is clinically significant even when the absolute value seems modest. Chronicity cannot be established from 48 hours, and kidney injury may occur before prominent symptoms.

questions.stem: Which additional finding most strengthens concern about the functional effect of rising creatinine?
options: Urine output falling to 0.3 mL/kg/hour over eight hours
Urine becoming pale after oral fluids
Stable nocturia over the previous year
A single episode of urgency after caffeine
questions.rationale: Sustained low urine output provides additional evidence of impaired function. Color and chronic or isolated urinary symptoms do not quantify filtration or current output.

questions.stem: A patient with rising creatinine had vomiting, poor intake and recent NSAID use. Which handoff best supports identifying reversible contributors?
options: Family kidney history, past stones, baseline nocturia and urine color
Hemoglobin trend, dietary iron, exercise tolerance and conjunctival color
Glucose trend, usual carbohydrate intake, body mass index and foot sensation
Recent fluid losses, blood pressure trend, urine output and medication exposures
questions.rationale: Recent losses, perfusion, measured output and nephrotoxic exposures directly address acute contributors in this scenario. The other histories can support a broader evaluation but do not target the recent deterioration as directly.

lessons.title: Glucose: low result
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: Glucose below the displayed reference interval.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess symptoms promptly and follow the local hypoglycemia protocol; the patient’s condition determines the immediate response.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: A patient has glucose 52 mg/dL, sweating and tremor. Which process best explains the symptoms?
options: Autonomic response to low glucose
Osmotic diuresis from excess glucose
Ketoacid accumulation from prolonged insulin deficiency
Fluid retention from reduced renal filtration
questions.rationale: Sweating and tremor are common autonomic symptoms of hypoglycemia. Osmotic diuresis and ketoacidosis are associated with hyperglycemic states, while fluid retention does not explain this pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with glucose 52 mg/dL is awake, cooperative and able to swallow safely. Which initial treatment route best fits a hypoglycemia protocol?
options: IV dextrose through an existing IV as the default first route
Intramuscular glucagon as the default first route
A mixed meal with protein and fat as the initial correction
Oral fast-acting carbohydrate with timed glucose reassessment
questions.rationale: When a patient is awake and can swallow, oral fast-acting carbohydrate is generally the initial protocol route with a prompt recheck. IV glucose or glucagon are valuable when oral treatment is unsuitable; a mixed meal absorbs too slowly for initial correction.

questions.stem: Another patient with glucose 52 mg/dL is unresponsive and cannot swallow safely. What change in management is most important?
options: Establish IV access before considering an available glucagon option
Investigate the last insulin dose before selecting treatment
Use the emergency parenteral treatment pathway and assess airway and breathing
Repeat the bedside glucose to confirm the value before giving treatment
questions.rationale: The documented low with unresponsiveness requires immediate treatment through an appropriate parenteral route and airway/breathing assessment. Verification and cause review must not delay correction; available protocol-directed glucagon may be used when IV access is not established.

lessons.title: Blood gas: respiratory acidosis pattern
lessons.notice: Read the units and reference interval before comparing the result. Check the clinical context and any previous values.
lessons.difference: Acidemia with increased PaCO₂ in this constructed example.
lessons.context: Synthetic adult example. Reference intervals and action thresholds vary by laboratory, patient and local policy.
lessons.nursingAction: Assess ventilation, oxygenation and consciousness and escalate deterioration. A complete interpretation needs oxygen delivery, history and possible mixed disturbances.
objectives: Compare the expected and changed finding.
Describe the finding without overclaiming its cause.
Connect the finding to a focused nursing assessment.

questions.stem: An ABG shows pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 26 mmol/L. Which primary disturbance best fits?
options: Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
questions.rationale: The pH shows acidemia and elevated PaCO₂ points to a primary respiratory cause. Bicarbonate is not reduced as expected in primary metabolic acidosis; both alkaloses would drive pH upward.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient with this ABG is difficult to awaken after an opioid and is breathing 7 times/minute. What is the priority?
options: Prepare protocol-directed opioid reversal medication
Repeat the ABG to assess whether carbon dioxide is still rising
Support airway and ventilation and activate the urgent response pathway
Administer supplemental oxygen and assess the saturation response
questions.rationale: Slow breathing, reduced consciousness and hypercapnia require immediate airway/ventilation support and urgent help. Oxygen does not by itself correct hypoventilation. Opioid reversal may be indicated, but preparation must not delay breathing support; another ABG is not a prerequisite.

questions.stem: Which repeat ABG most strongly supports improvement of the primary disturbance, assuming similar sampling conditions?
options: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mmol/L
pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 44 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L
pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 70 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mmol/L
pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 28 mmol/L
questions.rationale: Normalization of PaCO₂ with pH moving toward normal supports improved ventilation. A rising PaCO₂ worsens the primary problem; a higher bicarbonate with persistent hypercapnia does not demonstrate its resolution.

tutorials.title: Start here: purpose and limits
paragraphs: This tool is intended for educational purposes only. It should not be used during a medical response or as a reference for diagnosing, monitoring or treating an actual patient. In a medical situation, use your organization’s approved clinical resources, protocols and response team.

Some sounds and images may be optimized, simplified or exaggerated to make learning features easier to notice. Sounds and images are educational examples only and should not be used as references in medical situations. Individual source labels describe whether an example is clinical, simulated or illustrated and identify known processing.
These heart sounds are manikin recordings. Amplification and pronounced sound features can make timing easier to learn; loudness on a device does not measure severity in a patient.

This is an unapproved testing preview. Completing lessons or passing this quiz does not demonstrate clinical competence, award continuing-education credit or constitute nurse approval. Release beyond the authorized GitHub preview still requires the owner to verify three distinct trained-nurse approvals of the exact content version.

questions.stem: During a real medical response, a finding reminds you of a sample here. How should you use this tool?
options: Use the closest sample to choose an intervention, then confirm later
Use it as a bedside comparison if another nurse is present
Set it aside and follow approved clinical resources and the response pathway
questions.rationale: This app is for study outside actual patient-care decisions. Supervision or a similar-looking sample does not make it an approved clinical reference.

questions.stem: A sound or image in a lesson is especially clear or pronounced. What should you understand?
options: Teaching features may be optimized or exaggerated; real findings vary
The strength of the feature establishes the severity in a patient
A patient must match the example closely for the finding to matter
questions.rationale: These heart sounds are manikin recordings. Amplification and pronounced sound features can make timing easier to learn; loudness on a device does not measure severity in a patient.

questions.stem: What does passing this category’s quiz establish?
options: Independent readiness to use the examples for clinical decisions
Understanding of the stated learning limits, not clinical certification
Approval of this version for external release
questions.rationale: This is a learning check only. Clinical competence, accredited education and the owner-verified three-nurse release review are separate matters.
